newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spanish inflation ends 1996 beneath target.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spanish inflation ends 1996 beneath target.

text.p: Spanish inflation moderated to end the year beneath the government's 1996 target, but economists said on Wednesday the Bank of Spain is likely to wait for a further improvement before reducing its key interest rate again.
Prices rose 0.3 percent in December compared with November, for a 3.2 percent year-on-year inflation rate, well beneath Spain's earlier target of 3.4 percent for the year-end.

Even more importantly, underlying inflation, which gives a clearer picture of the price trend by stripping away volatile food and energy factors, improved to three percent in December from 3.1 pct in November.
The December fall in the underlying rate underscores a dramatic improvement during 1996.
The rate fell 1.8 percentage points in 1996, encouraging the Bank of Spain to reduce its key money market rate to 6.25 percent from nine percent at the start of last year.

But according to a Reuter survey of 10 analysts conducted on Wednesday, the improvement is not enough to prompt another key rate cut at Thursday's regular repurchase tender so soon after the last 50 basis point cut on December 13.
"The Bank of Spain has room to lower rates, but I believe that it will give itself time to see the CPI data for January," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.

Eight of those surveyed predicted the Bank of Spain would refrain from cutting on Thursday and would wait until it had seen January data -- and its progress toward the central bank's 1997 goals -- before again cutting rates.
Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato, inaugurating an economic seminar, said he was optimistic about the inflation trend in the coming months.

In a statement after the data, the Economy Ministry said Spain was likely to meet its 1997 inflation target of 2.6 percent set last September. The central bank's 1997 inflation target is not far off at 2.5 percent.

"Tomorrow they aren't going to cut rates," said Jose Ramon Nunez. "Since electrical tariffs are not rising we will get closer in January and February to the 2.5 percent objective and I think the Bank of Spain will wait."

Gwyn Hacche, economist at HSBC James Capel in London said he expected inflation in Spain to tip below three percent in January. Riccardo Barbieri of Morgan Stanley International said he saw it slowing toward 2.9 percent.

Pressure for an interest rate cut is coming from the currency market, which on Friday succeeded in pushing the peseta beyond the 84.00 per mark barrier and strengthening it to levels not seen since last May.
Peseta strength and tame CPI could persuade the Bank of Spain to move as soon as Thursday, Barbieri said.

"This could prod the Bank of Spain to a fresh rate cut of 25 basis points tomorrow, but it won't brake the bullishness in the market over short-term interest rates and it won't alleviate the pressure on the peseta," Barbieri said.
